issues.description: Within Experiment 1, the confidence scale is described in two mutually exclusive ways. The Procedure section states a 2-point scale, while Figure 1's caption states a 4-point scale. These cannot both be correct. This matters critically because the definition of 'high confidence' underpins every claim in the paper, and 'certainty' on a 2-point scale (rating 2) is categorically different from certainty on a 4-point scale (rating 4). If only ratings of 2 counted as high-confidence on a binary scale, the selection criterion is maximally coarse; if it was a 4-point scale, the paper never specifies which ratings qualify as 'high confidence.' This ambiguity compromises all analyses and cross-experiment comparisons.
issues.quote: Procedure: 'participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).' Figure 1 caption: 'she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty).'

issues.description: In the Experiment 2 results, the text explicitly states BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay in the follow-up ANOVA for non-illusory errors. However, Table 4 reports BFincl = 0.064 for that same effect. These values represent completely opposite inferential conclusions: BFincl = 190 is strong evidence for including Memory Delay, while BFincl = 0.064 is strong evidence against it. The text's interpretation ('Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay') is consistent with BFincl = 190 but is flatly contradicted by BFincl = 0.064. Furthermore, a BFm = 42 for the Memory-Delay-only model is also inconsistent with BFincl = 0.064, suggesting a copy-paste or transcription error that has corrupted the table, the text, or both. This undermines the credibility of the quantitative results in Experiment 2.
issues.quote: Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets (2% increase, from 10 to 12%, in both real and pseudo-letter targets). [Table 4 shows: Memory Delay BFincl = 0.064]

issues.description: The Methods section of Experiment 1 states that 45 participants began training, 5 were excluded on training performance, yielding 40 remaining participants. The Analysis section then states that a further 5 participants were excluded for insufficient high-confidence trials, 'resulting in an inclusion of 23 participants.' The arithmetic is impossible: 40 − 5 = 35, not 23. Either 17 participants (not 5) were excluded at the second stage, or 35 (not 23) were included. This discrepancy of 12 participants means the reported sample size is wrong in at least one location, making it impossible to determine the true analytic N. Effect sizes, power, and the meaningfulness of the Bayesian analyses all depend on accurate N.
issues.quote: The remaining 40 participants (28 female; age range 19-30 years, average age 22.2 years)... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded).

issues.description: In the Results section of Experiment 4, the text directs the reader to 'Figure 5' to examine error rates. However, Figure 5 was already assigned to Experiment 3 earlier in the paper. Experiment 4 has its own figure (labeled Figure 6 in its caption: 'Figure 6 Experiment 4'). This means readers are sent to the wrong figure when interpreting Experiment 4's data, conflating two different data sets.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA model comparison showed that the model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, Memory Delay...

issues.description: In Experiment 4's results, the authors state there was 'a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).' However, 5% > 4%, meaning pseudo-letter (mirrored) targets actually showed a LARGER increase, not a smaller one. This appears to be a direction error that inverts the finding's meaning. The error is particularly consequential because this comparison is invoked to explain why the three-way interaction was not supported.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.description: Experiments 1 and 2 contain no mention of pre-registration of hypotheses, analysis plans, exclusion criteria, or stopping rules. Only Experiments 3 and 4 describe a sequential Bayes Factor stopping rule. Given that Experiments 1 and 2 involve numerous researcher degrees of freedom—the 10-trial exclusion threshold, the choice of Bayesian vs. frequentist analysis, how to define 'high confidence,' which interactions to follow up—the absence of pre-registration means these decisions may have been made after observing the data. The paper does not acknowledge this limitation, nor does it report any Bayesian sensitivity analyses or robustness checks that would compensate for the absence of pre-registration.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor... [stated only for Experiments 3 and 4; no equivalent statement exists for Experiments 1 and 2]

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 both use sequential Bayesian stopping rules applied to the same critical test (Error Type × Target Type interaction), but use different BF thresholds: BF = 6 in Experiment 3 and BF = 10 in Experiment 4. No justification is provided for using different thresholds in otherwise conceptually identical experiments, nor for why neither value matches conventional stopping thresholds (e.g., BF = 3, 6, or 10 from Jeffreys' scale). The use of a lower threshold in Experiment 3 permits earlier stopping and increases the risk of false positives compared to the Experiment 4 criterion. This inconsistency also makes the two experiments formally non-equivalent in their evidential standards.
issues.quote: Experiment 3: 'once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.' Experiment 4: 'once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.'

issues.description: Experiments 2, 3, and 4 use a 4-point confidence scale (1 = guess, 4 = certainty), yet the paper never specifies which ratings qualify as 'high confidence.' This is the pivotal analytic decision in the paper: the entire argument that errors reflect genuine memory illusions rather than guesses depends on filtering by 'high confidence.' If ratings 3 and 4 both count as high confidence, the sample is larger and includes moderate-confidence responses; if only rating 4 counts, the sample is smaller and more selective. The threshold determines what percentage of responses is analyzed, making this omission a critical gap in methodological transparency.
issues.quote: As in Experiment 1, error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type (illusions... vs other errors) as independent variables.

issues.description: Experiment 1 uses a 2-point confidence scale (regardless of which version is correct), while Experiments 2–4 appear to use a 4-point scale. The General Discussion pools results across all four experiments to make unified claims about the prevalence of high-confidence illusions (e.g., 'Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms'). However, the operational definition of 'high confidence' necessarily differs between experiments if the scale differs, making quantitative cross-experiment comparisons of error rates invalid. Error rates will be inflated or deflated depending on how 'high confidence' is defined.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2) and up to 30% of reports when memory is probed at 3 seconds (Experiment 1-4).

issues.description: In Experiment 2, 92 of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded for having fewer than 10 high-confidence trials in at least one cell. This is a very high exclusion rate and creates a substantially non-representative analytic sample. The paper reports that excluded participants had lower average high-confidence rates (15.7% vs. 49.2%), but does not test whether excluded and included participants differed on accuracy, age, or other variables that might be related to outcome variables. If lower-confidence participants have different error patterns (as would be expected if confidence and accuracy covary), the reported results may systematically over- or underestimate population-level illusion rates.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.

issues.description: Across all four experiments, participants are excluded if they produce fewer than 10 high-confidence responses in any cell. This exclusion criterion systematically retains participants with higher overall confidence and removes those with lower confidence. Participants who have fewer high-confidence responses may genuinely be more uncertain about their memories, possibly because they have less robust memory traces or are less susceptible to forming vivid false memories. Excluding them removes exactly the population that would show the null result. The analytic sample is thus a non-random subset selected on a variable correlated with the dependent variable (confidence-weighted error rates), constituting circular reasoning.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis... Excluded participants had on average 26.2% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 3.6 – 47.7%, sd: 13.0).

issues.description: Experiment 4 was administered online via Neurotask on participants' own laptops, whereas Experiments 1–3 were conducted in controlled laboratory settings. The online format introduces substantial uncontrolled variability in display hardware (screen size, resolution, refresh rate, color calibration), viewing distance, ambient lighting, and distractors. Since the experimental paradigm relies on brief 250 ms presentations and subtle visual differences between real and pseudo-letters, these variables are likely to affect performance. The paper does not assess or report any quality checks (e.g., screen type, viewing distance estimation, response time distributions) that would allow evaluation of data quality. Comparing Experiment 4's results to those of Experiments 1–3 as replication is therefore problematic.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.description: Experiment 2's key manipulation—associating fixation-cross color (red/blue) with probability of pseudo-letter targets (25% vs. 60%)—relies entirely on implicit contingency learning. The paper confirms participants did not explicitly learn the contingency via a questionnaire, but provides no measure of whether implicit learning occurred at all (e.g., reaction-time sensitivity to expectation violations, cue-specific accuracy differences). The null effect of cue color is then interpreted as theoretical support for the claim that 'expectations need substantial time to develop.' However, an equally valid interpretation is that participants simply failed to learn the contingency, making the manipulation uninformative rather than theoretically meaningful. Without a manipulation check, the null result cannot distinguish between these accounts.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses. This experiment contained two memory delay conditions (short and long), two target types (real and pseudo) and two fixation color conditions (red and blue).

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the analysis plan states that cue color was a study factor. After finding no effect of cue color, the authors collapse across it for all subsequent analyses. This post-hoc decision to collapse a design factor after observing a null result is a researcher degree of freedom that was not pre-registered and not explicitly flagged as such. Had cue color shown an effect, the analysis would presumably have retained it as a factor, but the two-step procedure of 'test first, collapse if non-significant' inflates the risk of false positives in the subsequent main analyses if the null result was due to chance rather than true absence of effect.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors... Because of this, in subsequent analyses all data are collapsed over the two cue types (red and blue).

issues.description: All four experiments use Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs in JASP, but nowhere do the authors specify the prior distributions used. JASP's default priors for fixed effects (Cauchy distribution, r = √2/2 ≈ 0.707) can substantially influence Bayes Factors, particularly for small-to-medium effects. The choice of prior is especially consequential when interpreting BFincl values near the 'substantial' or 'strong' thresholds the authors rely upon. Without explicit prior specification, the analyses are not fully reproducible and readers cannot evaluate the sensitivity of conclusions to the choice of prior.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4, with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants were screened using a training task involving rectangles with different orientations (horizontal, vertical, oblique), and only those achieving >75% correct on this rectangle task were allowed to continue to the main experiment using letter stimuli. The perceptual and mnemonic demands of discriminating rectangle orientations differ substantially from discriminating real versus pseudo-letters: the former requires fine orientation discrimination while the latter requires recognition of familiar alphanumeric forms. Transfer of skill across these tasks is assumed but not validated, and the training-based exclusion criterion may have selected for participants with specific abilities (orientation discrimination) that are not strictly relevant to the letter-memory task.
issues.quote: Prior to the main experiment, participants were trained on a cued change detection task... the memory and test displays each consisted of eight white rectangles (0.05◦ × 0.01◦ in size) which had horizontal, vertical or oblique (45° or 135°) orientations... Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.description: The paper argues against response bias by noting that 'the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.' However, this argument is entirely qualitative and circular: the pattern interpreted as memory-driven is simply the observed pattern, which any single-process model could accommodate. Critically, no formal signal detection analysis (d' and criterion c) is conducted to separate sensitivity from response bias. A shift in criterion c toward selecting real letters—independent of memory—could produce the asymmetric pseudo-to-real pattern without involving any memory process. The complete absence of SDT analysis is a major gap given that the core claim requires distinguishing true memory illusions from biased responding.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.description: Throughout the paper, the authors use causal language ('world knowledge can shape memory,' 'expectations can reshape perceptual representations,' 'internal predictions increasingly dominate') to describe effects of time delay and target type on error rates. However, the experiments manipulate delay conditions and observe different error rates—they do not manipulate 'world knowledge' independently of the letter stimuli themselves. The pseudo-letter/real-letter distinction confounds world knowledge with multiple other variables (visual familiarity, neural representation strength, typicality, frequency of prior exposure) that are all perfectly correlated in the design. Stronger causal claims would require designs that independently manipulate each putative driver.
issues.quote: Together, these experiments show that expectations can reshape perceptual representations over short time scales... our finding that pseudo-letters are much more likely to give rise to real letter memory illusions, than the other way around, is expected: Memory traces for pseudo-letters are combined with strong internal priors for the real counterparts, making them more likely to result in illusory memories for the real letter.

issues.description: The authors argue that fuzzy trace theory (FTT) is inconsistent with their results because 'FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.' This reasoning is logically inverted: if FTT predicts that high similarity facilitates false memories, and the data show that false memories ARE abundant (pseudo-to-real illusions reaching ~30–43%), then the data ARE consistent with this FTT prediction, not inconsistent with it. What the data actually challenge in FTT is the symmetry of confusion (pseudo-to-real illusions are far more prevalent than real-to-pseudo), but the authors' argument conflates the overall prevalence of false memories with their direction.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant. Therefore, it seems that FTT cannot accurately account for the occurrence of this type of memory illusions in STM.

issues.description: The General Discussion makes broad claims about 'all stages of STM' being 'susceptible to illusory memories' and about implications for 'vision research' generally, including visual masking, change blindness, and motion perception. However, the entire evidence base relies on a single, highly specialized stimulus category: Roman alphabet letters. Letters are among the most extensively trained visual categories in literate adults and have uniquely asymmetric world-knowledge representations (real vs. pseudo-letters). The generalization to other visual categories (faces, objects, scenes, motion directions) requires empirical support that is not provided; the cited Chalk et al. reinterpretation is speculative.
issues.quote: The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research, as WM and IM tasks are often used to investigate the content of the visual percept for example in visual masking tasks or in change blindness tasks.

issues.description: All experiments used samples of Dutch university students, predominantly women (e.g., 51 of 64 in Experiment 3), drawn primarily from first-year psychology courses. The theoretical mechanism proposed—world knowledge about letter orientation acquired through 'lifelong learning and development'—would be expected to vary substantially with literacy, educational level, alphabet familiarity, and cultural background. Non-literate individuals, illiterate adults, or individuals using non-Latin scripts would have different world knowledge about these letters. The paper does not acknowledge this limitation or discuss how it constrains the generalizability of the predictive processing account.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet. Previous experience with letters should have provided participants with abundant evidence that letters typically appear in their standard form. This should provide strong internal expectations about the appearance of the letters of the alphabet.

issues.description: The paper states that symmetrical letters (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y) were excluded because they do not change when mirrored. However, it does not list which of the remaining letters were actually used as stimuli. Given that different letters vary considerably in visual complexity, similarity to their pseudo-counterpart, and frequency of use in the Dutch language (which could affect familiarity), this omission prevents replication and prevents evaluation of whether the chosen letter set is representative or introduces systematic biases.
issues.quote: Pseudo-letter were mirrored (i.e. flipped from left to right). Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays).

issues.description: Despite conducting four experiments with varying sample sizes, the paper reports no standardized effect sizes (e.g., η², partial η², Cohen's d, or the Bayesian equivalents) alongside any of the Bayes Factors or follow-up tests. Bayes Factors quantify relative evidence but do not communicate the magnitude of effects. Without effect sizes it is impossible to assess practical significance, to power future replications, or to compare the magnitude of effects across the four experiments. This is a basic reporting standard that is unmet throughout.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 1 was supported: Illusions (pseudo-to-real or real-to-pseudo) were much more prevalent than other errors (a main effect of Error Type, BFincl>1000). The interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay, (BFincl = 4.21) shows support for hypothesis 2.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, when the target is a pseudo-letter, it appears in the response display on only 50% of those trials; on the other 50% of pseudo-letter trials, only the real counterpart appears in the response display. This means that in approximately 12.5% of all trials, the correct response is not available as an option. The paper defines 'critical trials' as those in which both the target and its mirror counterpart are present, but it does not clearly state whether or how trials in which the correct response is unavailable are handled in the analysis of illusory vs. other errors. If such trials are inadvertently included or misclassified, the illusory error rate for pseudo-letter targets is systematically inflated, biasing the core results.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options.
